strengths: The paper addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: integrating slow-thinking text-only reasoners into multi-modal systems without costly vision-language re-alignment. The perceptual decoupling + reward-optimized captioning formulation is sensible and clearly articulated.

Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: seven diverse benchmarks, three MLLM scales (3B/7B/32B), comparisons against proprietary models, open-source reasoning MLLMs (MM-Eureka, VL-Rethinker, InternVL3-MPO, QVQ), and a test-time scaling baseline (VisualPRM BoN), using standard evaluation tooling (VLMEvalKit).

The plug-and-play scalability claim is well supported: models trained only with R1-Distilled-7B as the reward reasoner transfer to unseen reasoners (R1-32B, Qwen3-8B, QwQ-32B) at inference time with consistent gains, which is the paper's most distinctive empirical contribution.

Thorough ablation studies: component-wise ablation (tentative solution vs. captions vs. CRO), reward reasoner type/inputs, complementarity of CRO with GRPO, GPT-4o pairwise caption evaluation corroborated by human assessment (85% agreement), training dynamics, and extensive qualitative case studies in the appendix.
Good reproducibility: training data (ViRL39K), hyperparameters, framework (verl), and all prompt templates are provided in the appendix.
Writing and figures are generally clear; the Pareto-front framing in Figure 1 effectively communicates the scalability story.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: CRO is essentially GRPO applied to caption rollouts with a downstream answer-correctness reward. The perceptual decoupling idea and caption-then-reason pipelines are already explored in concurrent works (OmniCaptioner, Vision-R1, R1-OneVision), which the paper acknowledges. The technical contribution reduces to a reward re-targeting of an existing RLVR algorithm, which may be viewed as incremental.

Potential reward leakage / answer smuggling: several case-study captions (e.g., Table 11 graph isomorphism, Table 16/17) contain conclusions or near-answer content rather than pure perceptual descriptions. This risks the reasoner trivially exploiting embedded answers, inflating gains and contaminating the decoupling claim. The paper instructs the evaluation judge to delete solving processes, implicitly acknowledging the issue, but does not measure or control answer leakage in the caption reward itself.

The core assumption of 'lossless' conversion of visual information to text is not stress-tested. No analysis of failure modes on tasks requiring precise spatial/geometric perception beyond anecdotes, and gains on MMMU are near zero for the 32B model, suggesting limits of the decoupling paradigm that deserve discussion.

Inference-cost accounting is somewhat favorable: RACRO inflates total parameters by adding a slow-thinking reasoner (e.g., 64B for the 3B group) and generates very long captions (up to ~900 tokens per Figure 13) plus long reasoning chains. Claims of 'computational efficiency' should be weighed against end-to-end MLLMs at matched inference FLOPs/latency, not just parameter count.
Apparent baseline inconsistency: Table 4 lists Qwen2.5-VL-7B with average 44.5, while Table 1 reports 42.0 for the same model, which needs clarification and may affect the Figure 1 Pareto comparison.

Some negative or unstable results are not deeply analyzed (e.g., WeMath drops 3.4 points for 7B with R1-32B; MathVista slightly degrades for some configurations), and there is no variance/significance reporting for benchmark evaluations.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the motivation (avoiding costly vision-language re-alignment when upgrading the reasoning LLM) is practical and well-argued.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: seven benchmarks, three MLLM scales (3B/7B/32B), multiple external reasoners (R1-7B/32B, Qwen3-8B, QwQ-32B), comparison against BoN/VisualPRM test-time scaling, component ablations (Table 2), reward-computation ablations (Table 3), CRO-vs-GRPO complementarity analysis, plus GPT-4o and human pairwise caption-quality evaluations.

The plug-and-play scalability claim (training only with R1-7B but transferring to stronger reasoners) is well supported by Figure 1, Figure 5, and Table 4, and the observation that caption quality bottlenecks stronger reasoners is interesting and empirically demonstrated.
Training dynamics, prompt templates, and detailed case studies in the appendix support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core method is essentially GRPO applied to a captioning policy with a downstream outcome reward; the perceptual-decoupling/caption-then-reason pipeline already exists (Vision-R1, R1-OneVision, OmniCaptioner, etc.), and the paper itself admits these are concurrent or prior paradigms. The contribution amounts to a straightforward transfer of an existing RLVR recipe to a new module, which is an engineering contribution rather than a new algorithmic insight.

Gain attribution is a persistent concern. Headline numbers conflate (i) the benefit of attaching a strong external text-only reasoner with (ii) the benefit of CRO. While Table 2 partially disentangles this, the CRO-only deltas (e.g., +3.2 avg for 3B, +1.6 for 7B) are much smaller than the headline +12.9 improvement, so the 'state-of-the-art' claim rests largely on the external reasoner rather than the proposed method itself.

Potential train/test contamination is not discussed: the model is RL-trained on ViRL39K math/science QA pairs and evaluated on math/science benchmarks (MathVista, MathVision, MathVerse, WeMath, DynaMath), yet no analysis of benchmark overlap or held-out difficulty is provided.

The 'scalability / Pareto front' framing (Figure 1) compares total parameter counts but ignores inference cost, which is the practically relevant quantity: the system requires two large models in sequence with long slow-thinking rollouts, and no latency or token-budget comparison is reported against end-to-end MLLMs of equal total size.

SOTA claims are only partial: on several benchmarks (e.g., MathVista at 75.9 vs VL-Rethinker-72B at 80.3) the method trails existing systems, and gains on stronger base models (Qwen2.5-VL-32B, +3.8 avg) are considerably smaller than on the 3B model, suggesting diminishing returns.

The binary caption reward (answer correct or not) is a very sparse and coarse signal for captioning; the paper does not analyze reward hacking (e.g., captions that leak answers) or failure modes of the RL training beyond aggregate reward curves.

Some internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: the ablation table baseline average (38.4/45.3 in Table 3) vs Table 2 rows is confusing to cross-reference, and there are minor typos ('alingnment', 'prune to generate').

The stronger MLLM (32B) RACRO group omits GRPO 'because we obtain worse results than the original model after GRPO' (Appendix A), an unexplained result that weakens the generality of the framework and is only glossed over.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written: the perceptual decoupling idea (caption as an intermediate representation passed to a frozen text-only reasoner) addresses a real and timely problem—avoiding costly vision-language re-alignment when upgrading to stronger reasoning LLMs.

The core method (CRO) is sensible and non-trivial: applying GRPO-style RL to the captioner using downstream reasoning success as a verifiable reward closes the perception-reasoning loop and is well-grounded in the RLVR literature.

Comprehensive evaluation: three MLLM scales (3B/7B/32B), multiple heterogeneous reasoners (R1-7B/32B, Qwen3-8B, QwQ-32B) tested in a plug-and-play setting, seven benchmarks, and comparisons against proprietary models, reasoning-tuned MLLMs, and a test-time scaling baseline (VisualPRM BoN).

Thorough ablations covering component contributions (Sol./Cap./LLM/CRO), reward-computation choices (reasoner type and reasoner inputs), and CRO-GRPO complementarity. The finding that captions alone are noisy while tentative solutions act as a fallback is a useful empirical insight.

Additional analysis strengthens the claims: scalability of CRO across unseen reasoners, training dynamics (reward/length growth), pairwise caption-quality comparisons with both GPT-4o and human judges (85% consistency), and detailed case studies.
Good reproducibility: training framework (verl), dataset (ViRL39K), hyperparameters, prompt templates, and evaluation toolkit (VLMEvalKit) are all specified.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the pipeline is a straightforward application of GRPO to a captioning policy with a binary outcome reward. Caption-based decoupling pipelines and reward-from-downstream-reasoner ideas already exist (e.g., caption-and-reasoning data engines, OmniCaptioner, VisualPRM); the delta over these concurrent works is mainly empirical rather than a new technique.

Some comparisons are system-level and potentially unfair: the strongest RACRO results (e.g., 64B total with Qwen2.5-VL-32B + R1-32B) pair an MLLM with a large slow-thinking reasoner whose inference cost (long reasoning traces, multi-caption rollouts) is far higher than the monolithic MLLM baselines at similar parameter counts. No latency/token-cost reporting is provided, weakening the 'computationally efficient' claim and the Pareto-front argument in Figure 1.

The SOTA claim is fragile: on Qwen2.5-VL-32B several benchmarks decline (MathVista -1.4, MMMU -0.0/-1.1), and 'state-of-the-art' holds only on the average of selected math/science benchmarks; generality beyond these tasks is not demonstrated.

A nontrivial portion of the gains may come from simply injecting a stronger text-only reasoner rather than from CRO itself; while the ablations partially separate these factors, the headline comparisons do not always make this attribution crisp.

Potential reward-hacking/capacity risks of the binary reward through a 7B reasoner (noisy signals, verbose captions inflating context) are discussed only qualitatively; robustness across reward-reasoner mismatches during inference is not stress-tested.

The caption-only information bottleneck is inherent to the approach (dense charts, spatial layouts may be lossy in text); the paper acknowledges this but provides no quantitative analysis of failure modes tied to information loss.

strengths: Clear and practically motivated contribution: decoupling perception (MLLM) from reasoning (external LLM) enables upgrading reasoning without costly vision-language retraining, a real pain point for MLLM development.

VPO is a sensible RL formulation: using the correctness of the external reasoner's final answer as reward for the captioning policy, with a caption-penalty term that addresses an identified reward-hacking failure mode (supported by Figure 7 evidence).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: seven multi-modal reasoning benchmarks, comparisons against proprietary models, reasoning-specialized MLLMs, and prior caption-then-reason pipelines (ECSO, OmniCaptioner), across model scales (3B-72B).

Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2 and 7) that isolate the contribution of decoupling, GRPO, VPO, and the caption penalty, plus ablations on reward computation LLM and input content; includes a less common but valuable analysis of how the reward-computation LLM choice affects caption length and quality.
Strong demonstration of the inference-time scaling claim (Figure 10, Table 4): VPO-trained MLLMs trained with only R1-7B generalize across diverse unseen LLM reasoners, including GPT-OSS-120B.

Good supporting analyses: training/inference compute efficiency (Appendix D), general-benchmark checks showing no regression of general abilities, GPT-4o-judged and human-evaluated caption quality with inter-annotator consistency, and detailed case studies.

Transparent reporting: total model size includes the external LLM, checkpoint selection procedures are described, and limitations (domain specificity, frozen reasoner, no auto-thinking) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is modest: VPO is essentially GRPO applied to captions with a downstream-correctness reward, and caption-then-reason pipelines are well-established; the delta over ECSO/OmniCaptioner is primarily the tentative-solution component and reward alignment rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The headline gains (e.g., +11.2% for 7B) largely conflate the benefit of attaching a stronger external LLM; the ablation shows decoupling alone contributes +5.5%, while VPO only adds 2.7% over GRPO, so the core algorithmic contribution's marginal effect is comparatively small.

Some inconsistencies are under-explained: the optimal reward input for VPO (caption alone) differs from the inference input (caption + tentative solution), and this is only noted in a footnote without deeper analysis; likewise the claim that R1-7B is the best training rewarder due to caption-length effects remains speculative.

The caption-penalty mechanism (hasCap judged by the policy MLLM itself via few-shot prompting) is a somewhat fragile, heuristic reward component that could be gamed or unreliable, and its sensitivity to lambda is not studied.

Inference cost of the two-stage pipeline is non-trivial: perception generates very long captions (500-900 tokens after VPO) before the reasoner starts; the compute analysis in Appendix D.2 uses a rough proxy (model size x generated tokens) rather than wall-clock/actual hardware measurements.

Scope is narrow: focused on math/science multi-modal reasoning with verifiable answers; generalization to other domains (open-ended QA, charts beyond math, spatial reasoning) is untested, and the general-benchmark evaluation does not exercise the full RAPID pipeline.
Comparison fairness with prior caption-then-reason baselines (ECSO, OmniCaptioner) involves different backbone MLLMs and prompts, making head-to-head conclusions partly confounded.

strengths: The Perception-Reasoning Decoupling pipeline is practically motivated and clearly framed: separating an MLLM captioner from an external, replaceable LLM reasoner avoids costly vision-language re-alignment, and the 'plug-and-play' scaling with stronger LLMs is demonstrated across many reasoner configurations (Figure 10, Table 4).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: seven diverse multi-modal reasoning benchmarks, comparisons against proprietary, open-source, and caption-then-reason baselines (Table 1), detailed ablations of every component (Tables 2 and 7), and both GPT-4o-based and human pairwise evaluations of caption quality (Table 8) with reported inter-annotator consistency.

The identification and mitigation of reward hacking in VPO (the caption penalty, Eq. 3, with Figure 7 evidence) is an honest and useful empirical finding, and the analysis of which training-time reasoner best computes rewards (Table 3, Figure 9) adds practical insight.
Training and inference compute analyses (Appendix D) quantify the efficiency claims, showing large FLOP reductions versus full vision-language re-alignment approaches such as Keye-VL and InternVL3.5.
weaknesses: Serious methodological soundness issue: checkpoints are selected 'based on the average accuracies across the seven reasoning datasets (evaluated every 50 steps)' for both GRPO and VPO, i.e., model selection is performed directly on the test sets used for the main results. This inflates all reported numbers and undermines the headline comparisons in Tables 1 and 2.

Limited technical novelty: VPO is essentially GRPO applied to a captioner with a chained correctness reward plus an ad hoc penalty term; both the pipeline (caption-then-reason, e.g., ECSO, OmniCaptioner, PromptCap) and the RL machinery (GRPO/DAPO) are established. The ablations themselves show the largest gains come from simply attaching a stronger external LLM (+5.5%) and standard GRPO (+3.0%), with VPO contributing only 2.7% over GRPO alone.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable: RAPID results in Table 1 are reported with different, apparently favorably chosen reasoners per model (Qwen3-8B for small models, GPT-OSS-120B for 32B/72B), while baselines are end-to-end models without equivalent flexibility; the 'total model size' framing partially acknowledges this, but per-dataset inference compute of baselines under matched conditions is not fully controlled.

The 'tentative solution' component blurs the decoupling claim: the perception module emits solution attempts optimized by GRPO for answer correctness, so the boundary between perception and reasoning is largely rhetorical, and the reward leakage concerns (Section 4.2 shortcut behavior) suggest the interface is not as clean as claimed.

Generalization is narrow: the method is only validated on math/science-style benchmarks; the authors admit general benchmarks do not exercise the full pipeline, so the 'preserves general abilities' claim is weakly supported.

Writing and presentation have distracting errors (e.g., 'v-l alignemnt', 'reaonser', 'alginment', 'GPRO', caption penalty typo in Figure 17), and Figure 1 mixes models trained under different configurations in a way that is hard to interpret without Appendix A.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: replacing the reasoning component of MLLMs without costly vision-language re-alignment is a practical and timely question, and the perception-reasoning decoupling framing is easy to follow.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: results span seven multi-modal reasoning benchmarks, multiple model scales (3B/7B/32B/72B), and multiple external LLM reasoners, with clear comparisons to proprietary models, reasoning-specialized MLLMs, and prior caption-then-reason pipelines (ECSO, OmniCaptioner).

Thorough ablation studies: the component-wise ablation (Table 2, Table 7) cleanly isolates the contributions of decoupling, GRPO, VPO, and the caption penalty; the reward-hacking analysis (Fig. 7) and reward-computation ablations (Table 3) provide useful insights (e.g., stronger reward LLMs can reward brevity).

The plug-and-play / inference-time scaling claim is supported by experiments pairing one VPO-optimized MLLM with many different LLMs (Fig. 10), showing gains generalize beyond the reward LLM used in training.

Goes beyond accuracy numbers: caption quality is validated with both GPT-4o-as-judge and human evaluation (with reasonable consistency metrics), general benchmarks confirm no regression of general abilities, and compute-efficiency analyses (training FLOPs vs. Keye-VL/InternVL3.5; inference compute vs. accuracy) address practicality concerns.
Writing and presentation are generally clear; methodology details (prompts, hyperparameters, checkpoint selection, sequential GRPO→VPO training) are documented, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core technical contribution: VPO is essentially GRPO applied to captioning with an external-LLM correctness reward plus a heuristic caption penalty, and caption-then-reason pipelines are well established (PromptCap, ECSO, OmniCaptioner). The novelty rests mostly on the RL feedback loop through a frozen reasoner, which is an incremental but sensible extension.

The headline gains conflate multiple sources of improvement: the ablation shows decoupling alone (+5.5%) dominates, while the full VPO with caption penalty adds only ~1.0% over VPO-without-penalty and ~2.7% over GRPO-only. Comparisons against full MLLMs in Table 1/Fig. 1 include an external LLM's parameters, which makes the performance-size trade-off narrative somewhat misleading without the compute analysis.

Potential information leakage in the pipeline: passing the MLLM's own tentative solution to the reasoner may allow the LLM to simply trust or copy the answer (the prompt explicitly permits outputting the tentative response), so part of the gain may reflect the MLLM's intrinsic reasoning rather than improved perception; the paper does not isolate this effect (e.g., by ablating the 'trust the tentative answer' clause).

Benchmark contamination risk is not discussed: training on ViRL39K and using very recent LLM reasoners (Qwen3, GPT-OSS) on widely circulated benchmarks (MathVista, MMMU, MathVerse) could inflate results; no decontamination analysis or discussion is provided.

Some design choices are ad hoc and fragile: the caption penalty relies on the policy MLLM itself judging whether its output contains a caption via few-shot prompting; checkpoint selection is performed by evaluating on the same seven reasoning benchmarks used for reporting (effectively test-set model selection), which weakens the evaluation protocol.

The 3B model requires an extra GRPO stage after VPO to recover degraded reasoning, and VPO-alone can hurt reasoning (rows H vs. I), suggesting the sequential training recipe is unstable and may not generalize cleanly; the ablation tables for 3B and 7B also contain minor inconsistencies.

Generalization is limited to math/science reasoning; the general-benchmark evaluation does not exercise the full pipeline (LLM not activated), so claims about preserved general abilities are only partially validated.
No explicit statement of code/model release, which limits reproducibility for a systems-heavy paper.
